title: Bounding Two-Way Average Communication Cost of Simulating Quantum Correlations
authors: Kai-Siang Chen, Gelo Noel M. Tabia, Bo-An Tsai, Swati Kumari, Yeong-Cherng Liang
abstract: Bell nonlocal correlations cannot be reproduced by local hidden-variable models without communication, making classical communication cost a natural quantitative measure of nonlocality. Although finite communication always suffices to simulate any correlation in a fixed finite Bell scenario, determining the minimum amount needed to (exactly) simulate any given nonlocal correlation remains challenging, especially in the average-cost setting. Here, we derive lower bounds on input-average communication cost from nonlocal games, allowing variable-length, fully interactive two-way protocols. When applied to parallel games, these bounds yield explicit finite quantum correlations for which the exact simulation cost exceeds any prescribed finite input-average communication budget. For $n$ parallel Magic-Square-winning correlations, we prove a lower bound of $n\log_2(3/2)$ bits and give a one-way communication protocol that attains this rate asymptotically. For the quantum correlation maximally winning the $n$-copy of the Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt nonlocal game, we obtain an input-average lower bound of approximately $0.04627n$ bits for exact simulation. Finally, we formulate a hierarchy of lower bounds and complementary upper bounds using deterministic correlations up to chosen communication costs. Both recover the exact input-average cost at their final levels, and if the bounds agree at lower levels, their common value yields the exact input-average cost without needing to consider all communication strategies.
summary: This paper develops sophisticated lower bounds on the average classical communication cost needed to simulate quantum correlations in nonlocal games. By adapting communication complexity tools and constructing an LP hierarchy, the authors provide precise quantitative measures of quantum nonlocality. This work is crucial for understanding the resource theory of quantum information.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the minimum classical communication cost required to simulate quantum correlations, particularly in the challenging setting of input-average communication cost.
main_result: They derive explicit lower bounds for the average communication cost for simulating nonlocal quantum correlations, achieving specific bounds for parallel Magic-Square-winning correlations and the CHSH game.
method: The authors adapt communication-complexity techniques, utilizing rooted public trees and developing a Linear Programming (LP) hierarchy of lower bounds based on deterministic correlations.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on bipartite Bell scenarios involving Alice and Bob, comparing quantum correlations (from quantum measurements) against classical correlations achievable via communication protocols.
key_observables: Input-average communication cost ($ ar{C}_\sigma^\mu$), winning probability in nonlocal games, and the structure of communication protocols represented by public trees.
important_parameters: The number of parallel copies ($n$), the input distribution ($\mu$), and the specific quantum correlation being simulated (e.g., CHSH).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of an optimal finite protocol and assumes the input distribution has full support for key lemmas.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a rooted public tree structure used to model communication protocols and calculate the associated communication cost. Figure 2 shows a one-bit communication strategy winning the CHSH game.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing lower bounds from nonlocal games, then developing the framework using the winning-rectangle and winning-probability bounds for parallel repetitions, and finally introducing an LP hierarchy to approach the exact input-average cost.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, quantifiable measures (communication cost) for the nonclassical resources inherent in quantum correlations, which is fundamental to understanding the limits of classical simulation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. An example of a rooted public tree. Upon learning her local input x, Alice begins by sending one bit. Sending 0 ends communi- cation at ℓ0, whereas sending 1 passes the turn to Bob. Based on his local input y, Bob replies accordingly, which either ends communi- cation at ℓ10 when he sends 0, or returns the turn to Alice when he sends 1. In the latter case, Alice’s final bit selects between ℓ110 and ℓ111. The leaf subscripts record the complete message sequences. Since every internal node has m(v) = 2, the four paths leading to ℓ0, ℓ10, ℓ110, and ℓ111 have communication costs of 1, 2, 3, and 3 bits, respectively.

FIG. 2. A one-bit communication strategy that wins the CHSH game with certainty. Alice and Bob receive inputs x, y ∈{0, 1} and pro- duce outputs a, b ∈{0, 1}, respectively. They win when a⊕b = xy. Alice sends her input x to Bob and always outputs a = 0. Bob out- puts b = 0 if x = 0 and b = y if x = 1. The two middle grids show the corresponding local strategies on the full input space. Rows cor- respond to Alice’s inputs x = 0, 1 from top to bottom, and columns to Bob’s inputs y = 0, 1 from left to right.
